paragraphs: At the moment of its founding, each member gives himself to the community exactly as he is, with all the resources at his command, including the goods he owns. By this act, possession does not change its nature when it changes hands, and it does not become property in the hands of the Sovereign. But the forces of the city are vastly greater than those of any individual, so public possession is also, in fact, stronger and more irrevocable, though no more legitimate, at least from the point of view of foreigners. Toward its members, the State is master of all their goods by the social compact, which within the State is the basis of every right. Toward other powers, however, it is master of them only by the right of the first occupier, which it holds from its members.

The right of the first occupier is more real than the right of the strongest, yet it becomes a true right only once the right of property has been established. By nature every man has a right to everything he needs. But the positive act that makes him owner of one thing shuts him out from everything else. His share is settled, so he should keep to it and has no further right against the community. That is why the right of the first occupier, so weak in the state of nature, claims the respect of every man in civil society. What we respect in this right is less what belongs to another than what does not belong to us.

In general, three conditions are necessary to establish the right of the first occupier over a piece of land. First, the land must not yet be inhabited. Second, a man must occupy only as much as he needs to live on. Third, he must take possession not by an empty ceremony but by labor and cultivation, the only sign of ownership that others should respect in the absence of a legal title.

If we base the right of first occupancy on need and labor, are we not stretching it as far as it will go? Can such a right be left without limits? Is it enough to set foot on common ground in order to call yourself its master on the spot? Is it enough to have the strength to drive others off for a moment, in order to establish a right to keep them out forever? How can a man or a people seize a vast territory and keep it from the rest of the world, except by a punishable usurpation, when such an act robs everyone else of the home and the means of living that nature gave them all in common? When Nuñez Balboa stood on the seashore and took possession of the South Seas and all of South America in the name of the crown of Castile, was that enough to dispossess everyone who actually lived there and to shut out every prince in the world? If so, such ceremonies are repeated pointlessly, and the Catholic King need only take possession of the entire universe at once, from his own apartment, merely making a later reservation for whatever other princes already held.

We can picture how the lands of individuals, where they lay next to each other and came to be joined, became the public territory, and how the right of Sovereignty, reaching from the subjects out over the lands they held, became at once real and personal. This made the landholders more dependent, and the forces at their command became a guarantee of their loyalty. Ancient monarchs seem not to have noticed this advantage. They called themselves Kings of the Persians, Scythians or Macedonians, and seem to have thought of themselves more as rulers of men than as masters of a country. Those of today are cleverer: they call themselves Kings of France, Spain, England and so on. By holding the land, they feel quite sure of holding the inhabitants.

What is peculiar about this transfer is that, when the community takes over the goods of individuals, it does not strip them of anything; it only secures their legitimate possession, turning usurpation into true right and enjoyment into ownership. The possessors are then regarded as trustees of the public good. All the members of the State respect their rights, and all its forces defend those rights against foreign aggression. So by a cession that benefits the public, and benefits themselves even more, they have, so to speak, acquired everything they gave up. This paradox is easily explained by the distinction between the rights that the Sovereign and the owner have over the same estate, as we shall see later. It can also happen that men begin to unite with one another before they possess anything, and that they then occupy a stretch of country big enough for all, and either enjoy it in common or divide it among themselves, equally or in proportions set by the Sovereign. However the acquisition happens, each individual’s right to his own estate is always subordinate to the community’s right over everything. Without that, the social bond would have no stability, and the exercise of Sovereignty no real force.

I shall end this chapter and this book with a remark on which the whole social system should rest, _i.e._ that, instead of destroying natural inequality, the fundamental compact replaces whatever physical inequality nature may have set up between men with a moral and legitimate equality. Men who may be unequal in strength or intelligence all become equal by convention and legal right.[1]
